detail.check: fact.json {"select": {"unit": ["P"], "certain": true}, "statistic": {"page_group_similarity": {"by": "hand"}}, "compare": [{"null": "shuffle_page_labels", "perms": 199, "p": 0.01}]} after the code change is merged; then attack.json (fact) with the R-017 text.
detail.statement: Follows P-G-007 and P-G-008, public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. P-G-008 showed that the section cannot be isolated on a sample of 34 pages: sections are runs of neighbouring pages, so any text that changes along the book beats a null that deals section labels among whole pages, and the rotation null has no power. I confirm that for the section (page-pair similarity, same section minus different section: 0.053 on the evaluation pages but 0.011 and 0.005 on two samples of training pages). The scribe is different, because the scribes do not sit in runs: in the herbal quires Davis's hands 1, 2 and 5 alternate by sheet, so pages far apart can share a scribe while neighbours do not. Statistic: cosine of raw word counts for every pair of pages with at least 40 certain paragraph words; median over pairs written by the same hand minus median over pairs written by different hands (hand labels from Davis 2020 as carried in the transliteration header, a palaeographic label, not derived from the vocabulary; it does largely coincide with Currier's languages, which were derived from the text). Null: the hand labels dealt at random among the pages, every page whole (199 deals). Manuscript: 0.106 on the 34 evaluation pages (Takahashi 0.099, RF 0.086), 0.118 on all training pages, 0.061 to 0.175 on six samples of 31 to 38 training pages; p = 0.005 in all nine cases. Under rotation of the labels along the page order (every offset) the manuscript reaches the floor of that test (p = 1/n, 0.029 at 34 pages) on the evaluation pages and on five of the six samples, 0.0625 on the sixth, so rotation is reported here but should not be a pass condition at this size. Generators, laid onto the evaluation pages as the scorer does: the drifting line chain behind R-012 to R-018 (window of 20 public pages) gives -0.002 to 0.075 on six runs, deal-null p 0.015 to 0.51, none at or below 0.01; with narrower windows of 10, 6 and 4 pages, two seeds each, 0.040 to -0.007, p 0.045 to 0.67 (these six texts still meet every established fact on the practice split); drift-free self-citation, contiguous or sampled, is negative (-0.04, -0.08); the plain line chain of R-011 gives -0.07. So 0 of 15 generated texts reproduce it, and narrowing the window, the obvious way to copy more of the book's local detail, does not help. Why it may be hard to copy fairly: an attacker's lines are laid onto hidden pages whose scribe the attacker cannot know; a table fitted by position averages over the scribes that alternate there. Why it may still fall: a procedure with two or more tables that it alternates by sheet, as scribes sharing a quire would, could match it if its alternation happened to line up with the hidden pages, and the present attack format gives it no way to line up; that is a limit of the format, not evidence about the manuscript, and it should be stated with the fact. Not evidence of language: scribes with different habits or different copying tables give the same picture. A reviewed code change is on branch code-L2-page-group-similarity-fleet-fable (statistic page_group_similarity by section, language or hand; nulls shuffle_page_labels and rotate_page_labels; one test). Proposed: once it is merged, register the fact by hand against shuffle_page_labels at p 0.01 (no level, no rotation condition), then send the drifting chain unchanged against it and record the outcome either way.
detail.title: Pages by the same scribe share more words than pages by different scribes, pages kept whole: a candidate fact the drifting chain does not copy

experiment.json.summary: With every page kept whole, pages by the same scribe are more alike in vocabulary than pages by different scribes (0.106 on practice evaluation pages, p 0.005 on nine page samples), and 0 of 15 texts from the drifting chain, at four window widths, reproduce it; proposes the fact once the statistic is merged.

model.json.statement: Components were chosen by greedy forward selection under 4-fold cross-validation over scribe 1's public training pages only (pool: vocab, chain, position, letters order 2-5, copy windows 3/5/10/20/50 with 0 or 1 edits, templates prefix 0-3 x suffix 0-3), stopping when a component gained under 0.002 bits per word. Cross-validated: 11.31 bits per word against 11.75 for the bag of words and 11.40 for glyph trigrams alone. The same search run separately on scribes 2, 3 and 4 and on the whole text picked the same core every time (letters order 3 first; copy with a wide window; position; templates), with cross-validated gains over the bag of 0.39, 0.39, 0.58 and 0.38 bits per word; scribe 5 has too few training words. In every scope most of the gain is glyph trigrams alone, the word-to-word chain is selected late or never (under 0.01 bits per word), and the memorized vocabulary is never selected once letters order 3 is in. Negative side: nothing in the current component language gets much below a glyph trigram model (0.04 to 0.16 bits per word), so a production process is not yet separated from spelling habit.
model.json.title: Scribe 1: glyph trigrams + page-local copy (window 50, exact and one-glyph-changed) + line position + prefix templates + chain

detail.statement: I tested the stationary P-R-007 reconstruction on the public practice layout. I fixed seeds 1–4 for ZL and 1–2 for an additional Takahashi check. Turning off a reuse branch returns those draws to the ordinary glyph chain. Whole-word reuse alone meets all four registered checks (F-018, F-009, F-011 and F-016) on all six runs, with F-018 values of 0.966–1.065 bits and p=0.005 under the token shuffle. Both reuse branches together meet F-018, F-009 and F-011 in all six, and F-016 in one. Editing alone meets F-009 in four of six runs. It misses F-018, F-011 and F-016 throughout. Turning both branches off misses all four. Permuting section labels among intact practice pages gives p<=0.01 even in four of six no-reuse runs. Rotating the ordered section labels over the 31 eligible pages gives p=0.0645 for the manuscript on both transliterations, and 0.0645–0.1290 for the whole-copy condition. These practice checks identify whole-word reuse as sufficient for the original section statistic in this implementation. The cyclic comparison has yet to show whether it can detect vocabulary specific to a section at this sample size.

step.json.statement: Two independent ablations agree that F-018 does not separate procedures: fleet-sol's reconstruction of the drifting chain meets it with shuffled windows and even with one global table (1.11 to 1.14 bits), and R-017's own lines in random block order meet it too, so reuse of recent words is enough; a null that keeps pages whole does not rescue it (the generator still gives p = 0.005) and a null that moves section edges has no power on 34 pages (P-G-008). The most promising lead on the board is fleet-fable's P-G-009: with pages kept whole, pages by the same scribe share more vocabulary than pages by different scribes, and 0 of 15 drifting-chain texts reproduce it, plausibly because one scribe's pages lie far apart in the book (herbal and biological, for instance) where local drift cannot reach; it should be checked against Currier language and section before it is registered, since scribe, language and section overlap. Two blue-team predictions were checked on public pages and failed: labels share no more words, near-words, opening glyphs or stripped cores with their own page's text than with other pages of the same section (p 0.31 to 0.58), and the jar-versus-plant-part label contrast, though real on public pages, reaches p = 0.05 in only 3 of 36 hidden-sized samples. The two-sided Timm fact (similar words on the line above, at least 0.012 and at most 0.045, which the drifting chain overshoots at 0.051) still waits on code review.

detail.check: Rerun on public pages: median page-pair cosine for pairs more than 15 pages apart, split by same or different Currier language, section and hand; a scribe fact should hold within one language before it is registered as one.
detail.statement: A stratified check on P-G-009 before it is registered, public pages only (practice training and evaluation together, ZL, certain paragraph words, 202 pages with at least 40), median cosine of raw word counts over page pairs. To keep local drift out, only pairs more than 15 pages apart in manuscript order are compared. Same Currier language, same section: same hand 0.268 (3,678 pairs) against different hand 0.237 (241), a difference of +0.031. Same language, different section: same hand 0.274 (2,210) against different hand 0.317 (1,787), a difference of -0.043. Different language, different section, different hand: 0.158 (6,885). So almost all of the same-scribe effect over far pages is the A/B split: pages of one language resemble each other at about 0.24 to 0.32 whoever wrote them, pages of different languages at about 0.15, and inside a language the hand moves the median by a few hundredths in either direction. Two consequences for the fact. (1) It is still a fair generator target, and the reason the drifting chain fails it stands: pages of one dialect recur far apart (herbal B among herbal A, biological and star pages), so local drift cannot carry it. A procedure with two tables used by gathering or by sheet would pass, which says the text has two dialects that alternate in the book, not that it means anything. (2) Since the hand label nearly coincides with Currier's language, and Currier's language was itself defined from the text, the scribe statistic is close to circular as evidence about scribes; registering it with the language label instead would say the same thing more plainly and with more pages, and a scribe claim needs a test inside one language. The section half of this check also confirms P-G-008: same-section, different-language far pairs (0.147) are no closer than different-section ones (0.158). Scripts were local; nothing here is scored.
detail.title: Within one Currier language the scribe adds little: the same-scribe vocabulary effect is mostly the A/B dialect, measured on far-apart page pairs

check: Repeat P-G-005's document construction, rank-75 projection and matched line layouts. In each of four folds retain public training pages satisfying floor(page order / 8) modulo 4 equal to the fold number for evaluation, and exclude any window spanning an omitted page. Fit tables and the TF-IDF projection on the other folds only. Compute the bottom floor(0.05 N) per fold and match the validity mask before comparing CDFs. Form the pairwise discrimination statistic only from pages in the same fold. For the follow-up, freeze a generator that may fit changes in public training text but chooses its evaluation table using only the fixed writing schedule, with section and Currier labels omitted from its inputs. Compare both the CDF distance and the observed median drop and low-tail rank at label changes. Calibrate those scores on separate practice controls with known scheduled table switches and a wide range of transition strengths.

detail.statement: I repeated the P-G-005 TF-IDF/SVD experiment on four disjoint outer folds of the public practice-training pool, preserving consecutive page windows and fitting each model without that fold. ZL yielded 834 windows, with 15 section or Currier label changes and 57 other page breaks as the midpoint. Takahashi yielded 820, with 13 label changes and 57 other breaks. The manuscript's fold-specific bottom 5% captures 10 of 15 label changes in ZL and 7 of 13 in Takahashi. Pairwise discrimination at page cuts is 0.838 and 0.803 respectively, measured as the share of within-fold pairs where the cross-label score is lower, with ties counting half. The grouped line chain receives these labels for selecting its table, orders all cross-label breaks below within-label breaks within each fold in both seed runs and transliterations, and has higher overall median scores than the manuscript in every fold. The label-free positional chain has the smallest mean empirical CDF distance in both transliterations among these models (0.281 ZL and 0.308 Takahashi). It captures only one or two ZL transitions and three Takahashi transitions in the low tails. The global chain and the pinned self-citation model capture at most two. The global and grouped chains exchange their order by mean CDF distance between transliterations. These comparisons cover two fixed seeds per model and retain the limits of the small number of label changes. Matching a pooled distribution and matching the timing of the low scores are distinct checks.

check: Rerun on the public zodiac pages: same-position and best-cyclic-offset agreement of label sequences between every pair of signs, against labels shuffled within each page.

detail.check: Rerun on the public zodiac pages: same-position and best-cyclic-offset agreement of label sequences between every pair of signs, against labels shuffled within each page.
detail.statement: If the labels beside the figures of the zodiac roundels named the degrees or days of a sign (a common reading of the thirty figures per sign), the same words would follow in the same order on every sign, up to where each ring starts. Tested on the 12 public zodiac pages (ZL, all label loci of section Z in transcription order: f70v1, f70v2, f71r, f71v, f72r1, f72r2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v; 17 to 41 labels each, 350 in all). For every pair of pages I counted labels equal at the same position, and then took the best of every cyclic offset of one ring against the other, so a ring transcribed from a different starting figure is matched at its best alignment. Null: each page's labels in a random order (40 draws), the same best-offset count. Same position, no offset: 0.18% of positions agree exactly, against 0.06% to 0.29% at offsets of 3, 5 or 7. Best offset per pair, summed over the 66 pairs: 41 exact agreements against a null mean of 40.1 (p = 0.34); allowing one glyph of difference, 115 against 114.0 (p = 0.41). So nothing in the order of the labels repeats from sign to sign: they are not a fixed sequence of degree or day names written out in order, whether as whole words or with one glyph changed for the sign, and the ring order is no help as an anchor. Limits: the transcription order of label loci may not follow the ring exactly on every page, and names that change by more than one glyph per sign would not be caught. Several label words do recur across signs (otaly six times on four zodiac pages, okeey, okaly, otedy), but not at corresponding places in the ring. No anchor follows from this.
detail.title: The zodiac figure labels do not repeat as an ordered list from sign to sign, whatever the starting point

sources: Beinecke MS 408, IIIF canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006196 (label '68r', the three-panel foldout; f68r3 is the right-hand wheel); the cluster at full size x=4850-6150, y=1100-1800: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006196/4850,1100,1300,700/1300,/0/default.jpg

Zandbergen-Landini transliteration ZL 3b (pinned data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt), f68r3 page comment: 'Moon face in centre, 8 segments around it, four containing labeled stars, one of which probably the Pleiades'; star labels f68r3.10 dchol,day, f68r3.11 doaro, f68r3.12 oalcheol (locus type La, not Ls)

Stephen Bax (2014), A proposed partial decoding of the Voynich script, https://stephenbax.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/Voynich-a-provisional-partial-decoding-BAX.pdf : proposes that a word beside the seven stars on f68r reads as Taurus. I could NOT open this PDF from my environment (network refused), so I have not verified which EVA word he means.

Voynich Ninja thread 2102 (2017), summarized transcript of Bax's 2014 talk, https://www.voynich.ninja/printthread.php?tid=2102 : Bax says 'these seven stars might mean the Seven Sisters, the Pleiades'; the illustrating image is named 'DoarusComment.png'; the forum summary notes that the Pleiades/Taurus identification 'has been made by a number of people, including darkstar1 (January 2001)'
anchor.json.statement: UNCERTAIN; HERE IS WHY. What I checked on the scan myself (canvas 1006196, cropped at full resolution): in the upper-left segment of the f68r3 wheel there is one tight cluster of exactly seven small stars, drawn much smaller and closer together than every other star on the page, with a curved line (a tail) running from the cluster down toward the central moon face. Three Voynich words are near it: doaro immediately to the RIGHT of the cluster, on its baseline, nearer to it than to any other star; oalcheol written ALONG the tail line (ZL gives it a different locus type, La); and dchol,day written directly UNDER the single large star to the left, so it belongs to that star. So if any label names the cluster, doaro is the best candidate on the scan, with oalcheol second. The identification of a tight seven-star cluster in an astronomical diagram as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters, in Taurus) is conventional and has been made repeatedly (ZL page comment 'probably the Pleiades'; darkstar1 2001 per the forum; Bax 2014), but it is an inference from the drawing, not from any writing on the page. The pairing of doaro with a NAME is weaker still: the only published name proposal I know of is Bax's 'Taurus', and I could confirm only indirectly (the image name 'DoarusComment' in a forum transcript) that it concerns this word; I could not read his paper. Names listed: the Latin names of the cluster (Pliades, Pleiades, Vergiliae) and Taurus, because a label beside the Pleiades could name either the cluster or its constellation, and I do not know which. Recommendation to second-lookers: agree only if you can read Bax's paper and confirm the word is doaro, or find a second independent published source pairing this label with the Pleiades or Taurus; otherwise dissent with that reason.
anchor.json.title: UNCERTAIN: f68r3 label doaro beside the seven-star cluster (Pleiades, in Taurus)

established: In the full-page analyses, the NMF topics align more closely with hand and illustration groupings than the LDA or LSA topics. The authors report a close association between the astrology grouping, hand 4 and one NMF topic.

The 20- and 40-word experiments sample words within pages at fixed document lengths. They exclude the predominantly label-based astrological pages and other pages below the stated length cutoff. Some associations persist, and certain links change with the sampling choice.

The five-topic and two-topic analyses do not produce complete one-to-one correspondences with the five hands or two Currier categories. The authors discuss spelling, encipherment and word choice as possible contributors to what NMF captures.

The open long-range target is the A/B dialect: pages of one Currier language resemble each other at about 0.24 to 0.32 (median word-count cosine, pairs more than 15 pages apart) and pages of different languages at about 0.15, while the scribe adds only a few hundredths inside a language, so P-G-009 should be registered with the language label or tested within one language; the drifting chain fails it, a two-table procedure would not. Three label tests on public pages came back empty, all against the idea that labels name what is drawn: zodiac labels do not recur in the same order from sign to sign at any ring offset (p 0.34), labels share no more words or roots with their own page's text than with other pages of the section (p 0.31 to 0.58), and none of 205 plant-fragment labels in the pharmaceutical section equals the first word of any herbal page (against 3 to 5 percent for the second to fourth words). Next: register the dialect fact, then a generator with one table per dialect against it; the invented-language test (P-G-006) should start from these label results rather than assume labels name objects.

corpus.json.notes: License: the translator, Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, died in 1917 and Shakespeare's text is older still, so the work is in the public domain in every jurisdiction with a term of life plus 70 years or shorter; the item (https://archive.org/details/dlibra.kul.pl.38714_Esper--714-I_Hamleto---regido-de-) is a scan of a 1924 printing from the Main Library of the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) and carries no rights statement of its own, and no new copyright arises from a scan or OCR of a public-domain text. Why this text: P-J-004 asks for constructed-language references so the invented-language row of the hypothesis matrix has something to be compared with; this is the largest openly downloadable plain text by the language's author I found (Project Gutenberg returned HTTP 503 to an automated request). Size: 189,320 bytes of OCR; vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'conlang_esperanto') gives 166,501 characters, above the 150,000 floor. Content: verse drama, so speaker names recur (HAMLETO 453 times among the words) and lines are short; a short catalogue front matter for Zamenhof's collected works precedes the play. Most frequent words: la, kaj, mi, de, vi, al, ne, en, estas, li, as expected for Esperanto. Normalization drops the circumflexed letters' diacritics (c-circumflex becomes c), which merges a few pairs; that is the same treatment every pinned language gets. Named with the conlang_ prefix the step asks for, so it is never pooled with natural languages.

detail.check: Lay experiments/R-attack-F-018/fleet-fable/attack.json onto the practice evaluation pages with vs/redteam.py (cut lines) and compute the same-label minus different-label median page cosine for hand and for Currier language, with labels dealt among whole pages.
detail.statement: Check of P-G-009 against the text already on the record, before the fact is registered. I laid R-017's published lines and first_lines (experiments/R-attack-F-018/fleet-fable/attack.json) onto the practice evaluation pages exactly as the scorer does for a fact attack (vs/redteam.py, cut lines) and computed P-G-009's statistic on the result and on the manuscript: cosine of raw word counts for every pair of pages with at least 40 certain paragraph words, median over same-label pairs minus median over different-label pairs, against the labels dealt at random among whole pages (399 deals). Hand labels (Davis, from the transliteration header), 31 pages: manuscript 0.106 (p = 0.0025; the same value P-G-009 reports, so the statistic matches), R-017 text 0.071 (p = 0.015). Currier language labels, 29 pages: manuscript 0.122 (p = 0.0025), R-017 text 0.111 (p = 0.005). So the drifting chain is not far from this target in the format the scorer actually uses: registered at alpha 0.05 the scribe fact would fall to the existing R-017 text at once, at alpha 0.01 it would stand against that text by a narrow margin, and the dialect version would fall at either level. The difference from P-G-009's 0 of 15 is probably the layout: laid end to end onto 34 sampled pages, the chain's drift over the 20-page public window follows the manuscript order, and hand and language come in runs along that order on the sampled pages as well, so neighbouring sampled pages of one hand receive text from similar windows. This agrees with fleet-fable's own observation in P-G-007 that the contiguous layout lets local memory reach across sampled pages. Recommendation: register the scribe fact at alpha 0.01, state in its source that R-017's text gives p = 0.015 in the scorer's layout, and test it against fresh drifting-chain texts in that layout (and in P-G-007's whole-book sampled form) before calling it a fact the chain cannot copy; and prefer fixing the attack layout (P-G-007) before registering more long-range facts.
detail.title: In the scorer's own layout, R-017's published text already meets the scribe target at p = 0.015 and the dialect version at p = 0.005

practice.effect: At least four characters per eligible P word. Rank eligible positions independently per section with Python Random(26791 + 200 * background seed + page count), replace the rounded dose prefix in each section, and sample from four novel markers of the same length per section. Select one uniform marker slot per eligible index before applying any dose. The exact affected locations and marker multiplicities are paired with each placebo, created by shuffling marker assignments within length across affected locations using Random(78821 + 200 * background seed + page count). Fixed synthetic token counts and lengths within background and layout. Planted and placebo instances were shuffled within background and layout, scored under blind case IDs, and unblinded for aggregation after the score file was written.
practice.provenance: P-R-009 stationary whole-copy condition on ZL. The fitter uses the 68 pages remaining after reserving 124 from the public practice-training pool. The layout draws candidate pages with certain P words in the original corpus order using Python Random(408).sample and sorts prefixes of 31, 62 and 124 by original page order. The official practice-evaluation pages are unused. Streams preserve line order, with ordinary and paragraph-opening lines selected by the fact-attack rule and a four-word guard.
practice.statistic: F-018 mutual information of certain P-word identity and section. Verified to 1e-12 against the registered statistic on one unplanted seed of each layout. Token null shuffles all tokens before evaluating the P-position selection, as the registered DSL does. Whole-page permutations move only labels. Cyclic offsets include identity. Monte Carlo p-values add one to both numerator and denominator. Alpha is 0.05 for this calibration. NumPy default_rng with background seed plus 11091 for 199 token shuffles, plus 22291 for 199 label permutations. All three comparisons count ties toward the null.
practice.uncertainty: Wilson 95% intervals across the 20 backgrounds per case. For example, 0/20 yields 0–0.161, 2/20 yields 0.028–0.301, and 20/20 yields 0.839–1.

detail.statement: I ran the P-J-005 planted-effect calibration on 20 stationary whole-copy backgrounds per layout. At alpha 0.05, token shuffles and intact-page label permutations each rejected all 20 unplanted cases at each page count. Cyclic offsets rejected 20 of 20 unplanted cases at 31 pages, 2 of 20 at 62, and 0 of 20 at 124. Across placebo marker fractions, the cyclic rejection counts were 20 of 20 at 31 pages, 1–3 of 20 at 62, and 0 of 20 at 124. For section-exclusive marker replacement of 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% of eligible words, the cyclic rejection counts were 7, 18, 20 and 20 at 62 pages, and 0, 0, 14 and 20 at 124. The 31-page layout rejected all planted cases at every dose. Each page count uses one fixed layout, and the layouts are nested. They vary in section balance, ordering and paragraph structure. The calibration measures uncertainty across text-generation seeds conditional on these layouts. Differences across sizes combine page count with changes in layout.

detail.authors: Vladimír Matlach, Barbora Anna Janečková and Daniel Dostál
established: In the processed Takahashi transcript, the authors report positive and individually significant estimates for 90.1% of 760 lag-by-symbol tests over lags 1 to 40. The reported confidence limits are pointwise.
A Timm–Schinner generated sample comes closest to the manuscript by mean autocorrelation among the compared texts. The manuscript remains the maximum in that comparison.

The ligature loss weights were adjusted on Latin and Arabic examples, then fixed for an Armenian example and planted English and Czech examples. Each designated held-apart triplet ranked inside the authors' fifth-percentile criterion. The manuscript candidates remain hypotheses and in some cases the authors manually inspect discrepant occurrences.

open.check: Use paired public ZL and Takahashi samples. Freeze symbol preprocessing and measure Pearson gap autocorrelations over lags 1 to 40. Compare a global token-word shuffle with matched within-page line and paragraph-word shuffles, and with pinned self-citation and fitted stationary whole-copy controls on the same public layout. Report coefficients and an aggregate lag statistic against each null before interpreting pointwise significance. Estimate sensitivity with known rate changes and with known dependence at constant rates.
open.question: How much of the long-lag symbol-gap autocorrelation survives after controlling for local rates and the line layout?

open.check: Fix the published loss weights and candidate threshold. Evaluate all triplets both in public natural text with and without independent planted ligatures and in a stationary line-chain control. Record false-positive ranks, then check fixed manuscript candidates across ZL and Takahashi and use a separate public scan sample to evaluate disputed occurrences.

detail.statement: In the open PLOS ONE paper, Matlach, Janečková and Dostál propose a numeric encoding family after their symbol and ligature analyses. I reproduced the published toy demonstration: YZXAKJCCJBXX gives 222, 133, 113, 122 and the stated English word. The demonstration fixes a toy digit partition of nine Latin letters and a sequential three-digit alphabet. The paper's manuscript discussion leaves the EVA-to-digit partition, full glyph-expansion table, fixed reset boundaries, error policy and language open. The supplements provide an incidence matrix, discrepancy examples, ligature illustrations and a comparison-text list. I tested a narrow consequence of exact line resets: with decorative spaces ignored and no padding, every complete line must have digit length divisible by three after fixed glyph expansion. Among 615 shared certain paragraph lines on 31 public practice pages, the five highlighted decompositions give 201 divisible lengths in ZL and 213 in Takahashi. Expanded variants give at most 229 in ZL and 213 in Takahashi. The exploratory extended variant gives a one-sided p of 0.025 in ZL and 0.350 in Takahashi, before adjustment for the variants tested. The strict line-reset variants leave most lines with an incomplete triplet. This check applies to the fixed expansions and exact line reset. Continuous streams, other resets and an explicit padding or repair policy remain distinct hypotheses. A manuscript verdict requires a specified key.

practice.controls: Pinned G-self-citation, fixed seeds 401–406, trained on public pages outside the evaluation blocks, with the same certain-token line layout. Fit NMF and hand centroids separately inside every synthetic run. For a labeled positive control, replace 10% of eligible simulated paragraph words of length at least four by same-length words from four hand-exclusive markers per length, seeded by generator seed plus 997 times page order. The generators receive no hand labels for the unplanted control.
practice.data: Use the intersection of public practice-training ZL and Takahashi pages with at least 40 certain P words in both and identical section, Currier and hand annotations. There are 169 pages. Ignore labels and other units in the word features. Number canonical ZL folios in first-observed order, group consecutive sets of four folios, and hold out blocks with block index modulo four equal to the current fold. Both sides of a folio remain together.
practice.matching: Within each test fold, use pairs with different hands and at least two training pages per candidate hand. The main match requires the same section, a folio distance of 1–12, and a ratio of longer to shorter P token counts of at most 1.25 in both transcriptions. The strict Currier check adds identical Currier annotation. The wider Currier sensitivity increases the folio distance to 24 and length ratio to 1.50 without changing the Currier and section checks. Reused pages mean the pair scores are descriptive.
practice.model: Fit the dictionary and smoothed IDF on training documents with document frequency at least three, L2-normalize the weighted word-count rows, and fit a rank-five Frobenius NMF by positive multiplicative updates with NumPy default_rng seeds 47, 83 and 113. Use uniform initialization between 0.1 and 1, 300 training updates, and 200 coefficient updates for test pages with the basis fixed. Normalize topic rows and then coefficient rows, and use per-hand normalized means of the training coefficients as centroids. Given two candidate hands, compare the summed cosine similarity to the centroids of the two possible assignments. Ties count half.

detail.statement: I fit rank-five TF-IDF NMF and hand centroids on separate public blocks, then predicted the assignment of two known candidate hands to pairs of pages in unseen blocks. Among 2,022 eligible unfiltered pairs, correct assignments were 91–93% across both transcriptions and three fit seeds. In the 36 pairs matched on section, folio distance and length, correct assignments were 35–36 of 36 in each transcription and fit seed. All these matched pairs are botanical. The matched pinned self-citation backgrounds give 12–22 correct out of 36 in ZL and 14–25 in Takahashi across six generator seeds and three NMF fits per seed. Adding exact Currier matching leaves three pairs across five pages, all hands 2 and 5. Wider distance and length matching gives 14 hand 2 versus hand 5 pairs from 13 pages. The wider comparison gives observed rates of 57–64% in ZL and 43–64% in Takahashi, within the ranges of the self-citation controls. The dataset supports a comparison within the botanical section, with sparse support for separating hand from Currier over nearby pages.

corpus.json.notes: Second Esperanto text, to be pooled with C-052 (Zamenhof's Hamleto). Why it is needed: C-052 was added, but vs/facts.ref_langs() keeps only languages whose calibration blocks (every tenth block) hold at least 4,000 words, and Hamleto alone gives about 31,000 words, so Esperanto never enters a reference comparison; this text adds about 42,000 words. License: translator L. L. Zamenhof died in 1917 and the author of the preface and notes, Felicien de Menil, in 1930 (both dates from the archive.org item's creator field, https://archive.org/details/dlibra.kul.pl.39594_Esper--510-II_La-Psalmaro-el-la-Bi); the 1908 Hachette edition is public domain under any term of life plus 70 years or shorter, and the scan and OCR add no new rights. Size: 274,845 bytes of OCR; vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'conlang_esperanto') gives 228,336 characters, 42,085 words. Content: the 150 psalms in prose, with de Menil's Esperanto preface on Hebrew music at the front and short notes; the front matter includes a Hachette catalogue page and a list of sales agents in several countries (a few hundred words of place names). Most frequent words: la, kaj, de, mi, dio, al, vi, en, estas, li, as expected. Genre differs from Hamleto (biblical prose against verse drama), which makes the pooled reference less tied to one register.

Measured on the practice controls (fleet-opus): the search's best key scores far worse on its own trigram objective than the true key (clean -114447 vs -103058 bits; at 2% noise -121486, while a climb started from the true key reaches -111999 and passes (a) with +0.061), and its errors sit on h and c (German ch/sch). It is not a budget problem: 16 restarts x 6000 iterations, 4 x 12000, 4 x 24000 at noise, a letter-frequency rank start and simulated annealing (start temperatures 10, 30, 100 bits) all end in the same basin; one clean run at 4 x 24000 escaped. Try larger moves (swap the letters of two whole homophone groups, move a unit together with its most frequent neighbour, or restarts seeded from bigram rather than unigram rank) and report the German row with python3 -m vs season --parts controls, with the other languages' rows to show nothing regressed.

detail.statement: Esperanto is now pinned (C-052, Zamenhof's Hamleto), and on the practice evaluation layout it sits at the natural-language median on every word-level statistic we register: one-glyph copies of the last ten words 0.021 (manuscript 0.210, natural median 0.025), glyph entropy given two glyphs 2.54 bits (manuscript 1.94, natural median 2.58), edge-glyph dependence 0.125 (manuscript 0.230), singletons 0.674 (manuscript 0.711). So an invented language of Esperanto's kind, words borrowed and inflected, does nothing to explain the manuscript; the only constructed design that could is an a priori one in the manner of Wilkins or Dalgarno, where words are built from category roots plus one-letter modifiers, which would produce one-glyph variants in quantity, and that is the version P-G-006 should try. Esperanto does not yet enter reference comparisons (its calibration share is under 4,000 words); a second Zamenhof text is submitted to fix that. On the attack format, a code change in review adds cut 'book': the attacker writes a whole book and the scorer lays a random draw of its pages, in book order, onto the hidden pages, so long-range facts are no longer met just because text is laid end to end (P-G-007). Until it is merged, long-range facts registered against 'lines'-cut attacks should say so in their source.

detail.statement: The joint comparison the step asks for, at the manuscript's sample size: every text poured into the 5,461 certain paragraph-token slots of the public practice evaluation pages (as vs/dsl.py pours reference languages), edge-glyph mutual information (last glyph of a word, first glyph of the next, within lines) raw and shuffle-corrected (minus the mean over 10 shuffles of words within each line), and the share of word types that occur once. Manuscript (ZL): edge MI 0.230, corrected 0.180, singletons 0.711. R-017's published drifting line chain (fleet-fable; its lines in order): 0.178, corrected 0.128, singletons 0.713. Latin (pinned corpus): 0.073, corrected 0.024, singletons 0.722. Esperanto (C-052, Zamenhof's Hamleto): 0.121, corrected 0.061, singletons 0.666. An a priori code of the same Latin, built as a philosophical language would be (each Latin stem given a category root and a one-glyph modifier, each ending one glyph, EVA-like spellings, assignment by hash so nothing is fitted on the manuscript): 15 roots by 5 modifiers, corrected 0.003, singletons 0.296; 30 by 10, 0.002 and 0.516; 90 by 10, 0.004 and 0.626. The same a priori codes reach the manuscript's rate of one-glyph copies of the last ten words only when the roots are few (0.203 at 15 by 5 against the manuscript's 0.210, and 0.053 at 90 by 10), and then lose the singletons. Answer: of the procedures tried, only a glyph chain that runs across the word space (R-017) produces strong cross-word edge dependence together with a singleton-rich vocabulary, and it still falls short of the manuscript's edge dependence by about a third; no natural or constructed language tried comes near, and a code that builds words from roots and modifiers trades the near-copies against the singletons and produces no edge dependence at all, because the end of one word says nothing about the start of the next. practice.copy_controls: Use seeds 81–86 for both pinned G-self-citation, with exact certain-token line counts, and the reconstructed P-R-009 single-table whole-copy generator, with its two line streams and synthetic line lengths. Both fit public practice-training pages only and use the selected practice line IDs for evaluation.
practice.measurement: For each symbol compute differences of adjacent occurrence indices and Pearson correlations between gap vectors shifted by lags 1 through 40. Pooling uses a concatenation of pages. The page-centered version uses only gaps wholly within a page, subtracts each page's mean for that symbol, and pools within-page cross products and sum of squares at each lag. Use pages with more than lag plus one gaps and at least 25 aggregated pairs. Average coefficients equally across lags and across symbols.
practice.selection: Use the intersection of eligible P lines by ID from public practice ZL and Takahashi. Require each line to be nonempty with certain words made of acdefghiklmnopqrsty. Retain selected lines in original order and join words with single spaces within and between lines and pages for pooled estimates. Use ASCII EVA characters and fixed assay symbols acdehiklnoqrsty plus space, with at least 101 gaps in every evaluated case.
practice.simulation: Each run has 31 blocks of 120 gaps. Simulate independent geometric gaps with p=0.135 or alternating p=0.07 and p=0.24 by block. A correlated version rank-reorders the same gaps within each block by a standard Gaussian AR(1) with rho 0.92. Independently, the lag-20 check repeats the first 20 gaps of every 40-gap block. Use 24 NumPy default_rng seeds beginning at 61500 for the factorial and 47700 for the lag-20 check. Compare pooled means with 99 global gap shuffles and page-centered means with 99 within-block shuffles. These calibration cases use simulated gap vectors.
practice.text_nulls: Use 199 Python Random(71430) permutations for each text null, with global reassignment of words to fixed slots, intact line shuffling within pages, and word reassignment inside paragraph blocks in each page using the IVTFF opening/closing markers. Report one-sided larger-or-equal Monte Carlo p-values with plus-one correction. The fixed paragraph blocks preserve word counts and the inventories of each paragraph. Recombining words changes local character neighborhoods.

detail.statement: The 615 matched certain paragraph lines on 31 public pages give average pooled Pearson gap autocorrelations of 0.04458 in ZL and 0.04485 in Takahashi over lags 11–40. Global word shuffling brings the means to about zero (one-sided p=0.005 in both). Shuffling intact lines within each page gives means of 0.04755 and 0.04780, with one-sided p=0.975 and 0.985. Shuffling words within paragraphs gives means of 0.04934 and 0.04944, both p=1. The pinned page-local self-citation medians exceed the manuscript values. The stationary whole-line copy medians are around 0.003. After centering gap lengths within pages, the observed aggregate is about −0.014 and the paragraph-word shuffle p-values are 0.710 and 0.565. In gap-only controls, alternating page rates alone yield 24 of 24 global rejections and 1 of 24 page-centered rejections. Rank-imposed AR dependence gets 0 of 24 page-centered rejections at either rate setting. A separate exact lag-20 recurrence gets 24 of 24 page-centered rejections with equal rates and 22 of 24 with alternating rates. These results distinguish a pooled long-lag effect from residual long-lag dependence relative to the tested local controls, with demonstrated sensitivity to the specific recurrence used in the positive control.

established: The author places Voynich drawings beside comparators in named medieval herbals. The waterlily comparison includes British Library Egerton 747 f67r, Paris BnF Latin 6823 f109r and British Library Sloane 4019 f64v.

For f35v the author discusses the oak-like crown and roots and the discordant fruit-like clusters. The slides report Ethel Voynich's oak-grape suggestion from her notes and reproduce the black-ivy comparator in BnF Latin 6823 f60r. Both observations concern illustration motifs.

The author reports finding detailed resemblances while finding zero complete copies in the fifty herbals examined. He judges the page arrangement closest to alchemical herbals and treats the comparison as a visual assessment in need of specialist confirmation.

detail.check: Pour pinned Latin, Italian and German into the practice evaluation layout under the stated collapse rules and compute glyph_cond_entropy 2, single-glyph entropy and the dominant-position share; compare with ZL and Takahashi under EVA-basic segmentation.
detail.statement: Tested on the public practice evaluation layout (5,461 certain paragraph-token slots; pinned Latin, Italian and German poured into them, letters as glyphs) with fixed collapse rules applied in steps: voicing merged (b=p, d=t, g=c=q=k, v=w=f, z=s); then vowels to two (a=o=u, e=i=y); then l=r and m=n; finally a consonant skeleton with one vowel and h dropped. Conditional glyph entropy given the two previous symbols (glyph_cond_entropy 2, word space as a symbol): Latin 2.665, 2.656, 2.479, 2.394, 2.079 (alphabet 24 down to 9); Italian 2.576 to 1.966 (25 to 10); German 2.241 to 1.981 (26 to 10). The manuscript: 1.940 (ZL) and 1.936 (Takahashi), with 29 glyph units under EVA-basic segmentation, 19 of them at 0.5% or more. So a collapse reaches the manuscript's conditional entropy only when the alphabet is cut to about nine or ten symbols, and then the single-glyph entropy falls with it: Latin 3.91 bits raw, 2.35 as a skeleton; Italian 4.00 to 2.40; German 3.99 to 2.53; the manuscript keeps 3.89 (ZL) and 3.89 (Takahashi). The manuscript's drop from single-glyph to conditional entropy (about 1.95 bits) is larger than raw Latin's (1.25), and collapse narrows that drop (0.27 for the Latin skeleton), the opposite of what is needed. Position, measured as the frequency-weighted share of each glyph's occurrences in its most common word position (initial, medial, final or alone): manuscript 0.791 (ZL) and 0.793 (Takahashi), Latin 0.657 raw and 0.634 as a skeleton. Answer for this rule family: an encoding that merges sounds does not reproduce the manuscript's low conditional entropy together with its alphabet size, and it does not create the strong position-bound glyphs; what makes the text predictable is that most glyphs are tied to a place in the word, so a historically motivated encoding would need positional rules (as verbose ciphers or slot grammars have), not merged sounds. Limits: collapse rules applied to letters, not phonemes; one rule family; position-stratified bigram profiles reduced to one summary number.
detail.title: Collapsing sound distinctions lowers conditional entropy only by shrinking the alphabet; the manuscript keeps a large alphabet and is predictable through position

detail.statement: One independently specified procedure, frozen before measuring and fitted on no folio. Token formation: prefix + core + suffix, each drawn from a hand-written EVA-like inventory (20 prefixes, 23 cores, 21 suffixes, extended with simple two-part compositions to 60, 86 and 53) under fixed Zipf weights of exponent 1.2; no glyph-transition table is learned. Local reuse: with probability 0.25 a word is one of the last 15 words with one slot redrawn, kept only if the result is exactly one glyph from the source (a grammatical one-glyph edit); with probability 0.2 it is a whole copy of a word from 300 to 15 words back. Measured by pouring its words into the manuscript's certain paragraph-token slots (seed 1, after a 500-word burn-in) at three budgets. 2,000 tokens (training-page layout): manuscript H2 1.97, singletons 0.744, one-glyph copies of the last ten words 0.229, longer words already on the page 0.191, types 894; procedure 2.015, 0.663, 0.224, 0.093, 976. 5,461 tokens (evaluation layout): manuscript 1.940, 0.711, 0.210, 0.311, 1,907; procedure 2.079, 0.615, 0.238, 0.202, 2,123. 15,000 tokens (training layout): manuscript 1.959, 0.693, 0.219, 0.286, 3,740; procedure 2.111, 0.558, 0.243, 0.164, 4,406. detail.statement: Follows P-G-009, P-G-010 and the dispatch P-LEAD-008, public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. All texts below were written as a whole book (4,500 ordinary and 740 paragraph-opening lines) and laid onto every page of the manuscript, the fact being measured on the 34 evaluation pages of it (the layout proposed in P-G-007; code on branch code-R-book-cut-fleet-fable). Statistic as in P-G-009 with Currier's language in place of the hand: median word-count cosine of two pages of the same language minus two pages of different languages, pages without a language label left out, every page whole. (1) The manuscript. 0.122 on the evaluation pages (Takahashi 0.129, RF 0.103) and 0.109 to 0.191 on six samples of 32 training pages. Labels dealt among whole pages: p = 0.005 in all nine cases. Labels rotated along the page order, every offset: p at its floor of 1/n (0.029 to 0.031) in all nine cases, where the hand label missed once. So with the language label the stricter null can be a pass condition at this sample size, though with no margin: one rotation at or above the observed value would fail it. (2) The drifting chain behind R-012 to R-018. Laid end to end on the evaluation pages, as attacks are scored today, it does copy the dialect contrast some of the time: fleet-opus found 0.111 for the published R-017 text, which I confirm (seed 1; it passes both nulls), and over my six runs the values are 0.111, 0.077, 0.010, 0.106, 0.074, 0.095, two passing both nulls and one more the deal only. With the hand label none of the six passes at 0.01 (0.071 at p 0.015 is the nearest, as fleet-opus reports). Written as a whole book it does worse: 0.066 and 0.032 (two seeds), neither passing both nulls. Drift-free self-citation: -0.034. So in today's layout the dialect fact would fall to about one drifting text in three, and whether it stands depends on fixing the layout first, as fleet-opus recommends. (3) The generator P-LEAD-008 asks for, one table per dialect: the same chain and reuse rules, with three tables fitted on the public pages labelled A, B and unlabelled, and at each point of the book the table of the public page that lies there. That choice matches the evaluation page's own label for 29 of 34 pages. It still meets all 17 established facts on five of five texts checked. On the dialect statistic: 0.054, -0.004, 0.002 with the whole-text table mixed in at weight 0.1; 0.075 and 0.044 without the mix; 0.042 and 0.041 without the mix and with longer context (3 draws in 10 on two glyphs of context in place of 6 in 10). None of the seven passes both nulls (two pass one each). These are whole-book texts; I did not run the per-dialect chain end to end. (4) Why. Broken down by pair, evaluation pages: manuscript A-A 0.264, B-B 0.335, A-B 0.148; per-dialect generator A-A 0.28 to 0.30, B-B 0.38 to 0.44, A-B 0.26 to 0.32. Its pages of one dialect are as alike as the manuscript's; its pages of different dialects are far too alike. The commonest words it writes are the same short ones in both dialects (ol, or, ar, aiin lead both lists, chedy turns up among A's commonest), where the manuscript's lists barely overlap (A: daiin, chol, s, shol, dar; B: chedy, shedy, qokedy, ol, qokain). A glyph chain spreads each dialect's probability over many short strings both tables allow, and whole-word reuse then carries them across a change of table. So the open target is sharper than 'two tables': the manuscript's two dialects differ in their commonest whole words, and a glyph-level procedure with dialect tables does not reproduce that. What would: a word list per dialect (a table of whole words), which is a different procedure and should be judged against F-013 and F-014, which word lists tend to fail. Limits: seven texts, one way of choosing the table; the attack format gives a generator no label for hidden pages, so 5 of 34 pages get the wrong table, which lowers its score somewhat (not from 0.12 to 0.04). Proposed: once branch code-L2-page-group-similarity-fleet-fable is merged, register the fact by language against shuffle_page_labels at p 0.01 and rotate_page_labels at p 0.05; then send the per-dialect chain against it as a whole book, expecting it to fail, and a per-dialect word-list procedure as the stronger attack.

detail.statement: Three open questions were measured on the practice split this hour, each with the manuscript's token layout. Sound-collapsing encodings of Latin, Italian and German reach the manuscript's conditional glyph entropy (1.94 bits) only by cutting the alphabet to nine or ten symbols and the single-glyph entropy to about 2.4 bits, while the manuscript keeps 3.9 bits and ties 79% of glyph occurrences to one word position (Latin 66%) (K-014-open-1). A hand-written slot grammar with grammatical one-glyph edits and whole-word reuse matches the entropy and the near-copies without learning any transition table, but not the singletons (0.62 against 0.71) or the within-page reuse (0.20 against 0.31), and the gap grows with text size (K-008-open-1). Latin, Esperanto and a priori root-and-modifier codes of Latin give almost none of the cross-word edge dependence (shuffle-corrected 0.00 to 0.06 against 0.18), while R-017's learned chain gives most of it (K-001-open-2). The common thread: the manuscript is predictable because its glyphs are bound to positions inside the word and across the word space, a property of how the text was written down, which a chain learned from the pages copies and no lexicon or grammar tried here produces. Esperanto now has two pinned texts and enters reference comparisons. Next: the invented-language test should start from a writing rule that binds word ends to the next word's start, not from a lexicon; the scribe fact (P-G-009) at alpha 0.01; and the book-form attack cut once reviewed.

practice.data: Manuscript comparison uses shared certain paragraph-line IDs from official public practice ZL and Takahashi with all certain words as transcribed. Each pinned natural control is a cleaned lowercase ASCII prefix of 31,350 symbols including spaces. For each preselected pair, replace every nonoverlapping occurrence by a new atomic symbol X in a separate copy of the control. At most one such substitution process is planted per sample. The copying controls use the P-R-009 stationary line chain fit on public practice-training ZL, seeds 421–426, over the public practice layout. The line chain emits EVA-basic units directly. The reported fixed manuscript candidates occur as separate emitted EVA units where relevant to the cited false positives.
practice.eligibility: Candidate universe uses non-space symbols with relative incidence greater than 500/229431, matching the published absolute threshold after scaling to this sample length. Space remains in the transition matrix. For the special n → i plus space test and below-threshold signs, calculate their percentile against the same universe and mark them as noncompeting. practice.score: Use the printed weighted sum and exactly 1,100,1,1,100,1,1,10 as the eight weights. Estimate joint adjacent symbol frequencies with single spaces and zero a transition whose share of the originating row or receiving column is less than 0.002. For literal Rule 3, sum rarer-sign left-context mass where the commoner sign is observed. For the reconstruction sum the complementary mass, and replace Rule 6 (1−minimum candidate probability)/maximum symbol probability by 1−(minimum candidate probability/maximum symbol probability). The alternative is an explicit reconstruction. For Rule 4 with fewer than two realized contexts set loss zero, and treat other undefined Pearson coefficients as zero correlation. Score all ordered triples with C distinct from either component. Retain the same-symbol penalty when A equals B.

detail.statement: The printed Rule 6 in Matlach, Janečková and Dostál has a loss of at least 1 for distinct candidates, since the largest symbol probability and the smaller candidate probability sum to at most 1. Table 5 reports smaller Rule 6 values, including 0.299, with Rule 6 weight 1. In Rule 3 the equation sums probability in shared contexts and the prose describes the mass in unmatched contexts. I retained all eight weights and compared the literal equations with one plausible reconstruction of Rules 3 and 6. In both calculations five of six fully planted triplets that remained in the eligible alphabet ranked below the fifth percentile across matched English, Latin and Italian controls. Three other plants could not enter the candidate universe because the replacement or a component fell below frequency support. In unmodified natural controls 9–12 candidate symbols acquired a fifth-percentile triplet even though no ligatures were inserted. In six stationary whole-copy line-chain controls 10–13 of 17 symbols did so. More specifically, m with components i,d and q with i,e rank below the fifth percentile in both public ZL and Takahashi and in all six line-chain controls under both reconstructions. Those control glyphs are emitted directly without the tested pair-to-glyph substitutions. Three separate Yale scan checks also confirm real differences across the pinned transcriptions at disputed raw pair occurrences. The published percentile measures the rank among scored candidates and can be low for an explicitly unfused symbol.

practice.method: Generate 640 symbols per run from A–E using Python Random for seeds 2025–2056. For independent controls choose uniformly or with weights .40,.35,.10,.08,.07. For the sticky control use those same weighted draws with a 0.55 chance to replace each subsequent draw with the preceding output. Compare one-symbol counts to uniform expected counts using chi-square with four degrees of freedom at alpha .05. For the transition statistic compute Pearson over the adjacent pair table using the product of observed row and column marginals. Use 199 whole-sequence permutations seeded with replicate seed plus 5717, and count ties with the plus-one correction. This transition permutation preserves global marginal frequencies and is a concrete control interpretation of the paper’s illustrative transition comparison.

detail.statement: I audited the full version of arXiv:2505.02261v1, extending the abstract-level P-R-001 note. The illustrated validation reports a three-branch plant on f74r and reports claimed properties of f74v in Test 10. Folio 74 is excised. The pinned Yale manifest passes from f73v to f75r, and the public folio study documents the cut stub. These reported results need corrected folio identifiers and traceable crops. Test 1 reports seven radial spiral arms on f57v. On the public Yale scan I count four circular text bands and four short radial writing loci. ZL, Takahashi and Friedman each have four circular and four radial loci. Their radial word counts are 1,1,1,2. The paper leaves the boundaries of its seven asserted clusters unspecified. The chi-square section gives worked illustrations. Test 1’s printed counts yield 51.9, while the paper gives 54.2, and both exceed the ordinary five-category uniform critical value. I tested that uniform check and a fixed-marginal transition permutation control on toy random symbol sequences. All 32 nonuniform independent samples reject uniformity, and all 32 sticky Markov samples reject transition independence. The paper’s statistical comparisons can detect these generic forms of structure. An adjudicable test of the particular proposal requires fixed definitions of symbol roles, glyph groups and folio regions, as well as observed counts and a matched baseline.

detail.statement: Measured on the practice evaluation layout (5,461 certain paragraph-token slots, letters as glyphs for the reference texts). Pinned Latin and Italian with their spaces removed and re-inserted by a fixed positional rule (a break after one of a set of letters with a fixed probability: after vowels at 0.5 or 0.35, after s m t n r l at 0.6, after vowels or m n s at 0.4; seed 1), so the spaces no longer mark words. Edge-glyph mutual information within lines: Latin 0.185 to 0.280, Italian 0.142 to 0.332, against the manuscript's 0.230 and Latin's 0.073 with its own spaces; so a writing in which spaces fall inside a continuous stream reproduces the cross-word edge dependence with no further mechanism. The same texts do not reproduce F-010: edge dependence within lines minus across line breaks (edge_mi_break) is -0.006 to 0.027 for Latin and -0.034 to 0.047 for Italian, against 0.173 for the manuscript, because the stream runs on from one line into the next. They also miss everything else: conditional glyph entropy 2.83 to 3.04 (manuscript 1.94), singletons 0.85 to 0.91 (0.71), one-glyph copies of recent words 0.006 to 0.015 (0.21). Answer to the step, for this family: re-spacing explains within-line edge dependence but not its discontinuity at line breaks; a single process that gives both must restart at each line, as the line-restarting chain of R-008 to R-017 does, so the line, not the word or the space-delimited token, behaves as the unit the text was composed in. The separator part of the question (certain against uncertain spaces) is not addressed. Practice split only.
detail.title: Spaces that are not word breaks give the edge dependence for free, but not its collapse at line breaks: the line, not the word, is the unit

detail.statement: I checked Herrmann's open arXiv v2, sections 2–3 and Appendices A–C. The abstract disclaims a translation of the manuscript as a whole. The catalogue phrase that the author explicitly refrains from translation needs that scope. Section 3.4 gives an explicitly word-by-word gloss for a short sequence on f77v. Appendix C proposes a translation of much of the f116v colophon and labels it highly speculative. Section 2 also separates six direct reversals from two matches involving a diacritic and three further matches requiring other rotations or reflection, for a total of eleven claimed similarities. Appendix B uses different treatments of leading o in different words, and explicitly marks inserted and ignored characters. Appendix A drops initial signs in two tentative matches. These are documented editorial choices affecting whether Tables 1–2 can be frozen as a deterministic manuscript-wide key. The catalogue's broader description of the alphabet hypothesis and selected lexical examples agrees with the paper.

detail.statement: One more practice result joins the last three: Latin and Italian with their spaces removed and re-inserted by a positional rule match the manuscript's within-line edge dependence (0.14 to 0.33 against 0.23) but show no drop at line breaks (-0.03 to 0.05 against 0.17), so the edge facts say that spaces need not mark words and that each line was written as a fresh unit; a meaningful text could only meet them if its lines were composed separately, as entries, labels or verses are. That narrows what a reading must explain: positional glyphs inside the word, dependence across the space, a restart at every line, reuse of altered nearby words, and a singleton-rich vocabulary all at once; no language, constructed language, sound-collapsing code or hand-written grammar tested so far gets more than two of these. A grid key was sent into conlang_esperanto; constructed languages are pinned as references for the hypothesis matrix (P-J-004), not as candidates, so their grid cells should be closed rather than worked. Priorities unchanged: the invented-language test built on a line-restarting writing rule (P-G-006), the scribe fact at alpha 0.01 (P-G-009), and the book-form attack cut and the Timm line_near_excess statistic, both waiting for review.

A grid key was sent into conlang_esperanto; constructed languages are pinned as references for the hypothesis matrix (P-J-004), not as candidates, so their grid cells should be closed rather than worked. Priorities unchanged: the invented-language test built on a line-restarting writing rule (P-G-006), the scribe fact at alpha 0.01 (P-G-009), and the book-form attack cut and the Timm line_near_excess statistic, both waiting for review.

detail.statement: Corrects the second conclusion of P-G-007 (mine). Public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. P-G-007 said that reuse alone, with no change fixed in advance, does not make neighbouring pages more alike than distant ones once the book is sampled honestly, on the strength of one setting (a quarter of words written again whole from the last 300) failing F-011 on two seeds of three. That was too strong. All texts here are whole books (4,500 ordinary and 740 paragraph-opening lines) laid onto every page of the manuscript and measured on the 34 evaluation pages of it, which is my proposed whole-book layout (branch code-R-book-cut-fleet-fable; fleet-opus's variant on code-P-G-007-fleet-opus draws book pages at random instead and I have not run these texts through it). The procedure is the chain behind R-012 to R-018 with ONE glyph table fitted on all public training pages: no drift, no window, nothing fitted by position, no label used. Its only memory is reuse at the start of a word: with probability 0.20 one of the last 15 words with one glyph changed, and with probability 0.45 (0.25 before) a word standing at least twice among the last 300 words, written again whole. Result: all 17 established facts hold on 3 of 3 seeds. F-011 0.060, 0.043, 0.058 (manuscript 0.074); F-016 0.32 to 0.34 (0.31); F-014 0.69 to 0.70 (0.71, line 0.667); F-007 0.24 to 0.25 (0.21); F-017 0.004 to 0.019 (0.011, bound 0.025); F-013 1.84 to 1.87 bits (1.94, bound 2.1); F-001 14 to 31 (61.6, line 10). Neighbouring settings, one table throughout: whole-word reuse 0.25 from 300 words, F-011 holds on 1 seed of 2 (0.052, -0.006); 0.35 from 300, fails (0.013); 0.35 from 1,000, holds on 2 of 3 (0.049, 0.004 failing, third passing); 0.25 from 1,000 with a word needing three occurrences, fails F-011 and F-016. So the neighbour effect grows with the share of whole-word reuse, as a rich-get-richer process would have it: a word written again stays familiar, and the stock of familiar words wanders slowly enough to span fifteen pages of a book. Answer to K-003-open-1 as it now stands: a self-citation process needs no change fixed in advance at page or section boundaries, and no table that moves along the book, to meet every fact on the record, F-009, F-011, F-016 and F-018 included. The drift fitted on public pages in R-012 to R-018 was sufficient but not necessary. What it does not reach: the dialect contrast of P-G-009 (same-language minus different-language page similarity, pages whole). The one-table text gives -0.019, -0.042, -0.036 against the manuscript's 0.122, failing both page-keeping nulls on all three seeds, as it must, since nothing in it knows of two dialects. With the per-dialect chain of my P-G-009 follow-up (0.00 to 0.08, none of seven passing both nulls) that makes the dialect contrast the only measured property on the board that no procedure of this family reproduces in the whole-book layout. Limits: three seeds for the main setting, one or two for the others; F-011 passes its shuffle at small values (a toy text scoring exactly 0 passed it once in testing), so its pass or fail near zero is noisy and a level would make it firmer; the settings were chosen by looking at practice results, so the 3 of 3 is an upper estimate until it is sent once to the hidden pages. Proposed: when a whole-book layout is merged, send this one-table text unchanged as the generator test (it is the simplest procedure yet that meets every fact locally), and register the dialect fact as proposed.

detail.statement: Amends two statements of mine made earlier today: that a chain with one table per dialect does not copy the dialect contrast (my previous note under P-G-009), and that the contrast is out of reach of this family of procedures (correction under P-G-007). Public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages; whole-book layout as in those notes (branch code-R-book-cut-fleet-fable). The earlier per-dialect chain kept a single memory, so the words it reused crossed every change of table and its two dialects shared their commonest words. Change: each table keeps its own memory (its own last 15 words and its own last 300 words for whole-word reuse), as two scribes with separate habits would; whole-word reuse at 0.45 and one-glyph reuse at 0.20 as in the one-table text of the P-G-007 correction; three tables (public pages labelled A, B, unlabelled), the table at each point of the book being that of the public page lying there (right for 29 of 34 evaluation pages). No rule names a word or a glyph. Result on three seeds: all 17 established facts hold on 3 of 3; the dialect contrast is 0.127, 0.080, 0.110 against the manuscript's 0.122; labels dealt among whole pages, p at or below 0.01 on 2 of 3; labels rotated along the page order, at or below 0.05 on 0 of 3. So the level is reproduced, and of the two nulls proposed for the fact only the rotation still separates the manuscript from this procedure, and the rotation has no margin at 34 pages (its floor is 1/n, and the manuscript sits exactly on the floor). What this says about the manuscript: the dialect contrast needs two stocks of habitual words kept apart, which two writers, or one writer on two occasions, or two source tables would each give; it does not need language. What it says about the proposed fact: registered against the deal null alone it would probably fall to this generator on the first try; registered with the rotation it may stand, but could also fail for the manuscript itself on the hidden sample. Recommendation: register it with both nulls and say so, and treat a survival as weak. Caveat on fairness: the procedure uses the public pages' language labels to choose its table by position; that is the same licence the drifting chain took with its window, and fleet-opus's variant of the whole-book layout (pages drawn at random) would deny it, so the outcome depends on which layout is merged. Limits: three seeds, one setting, chosen after seeing the single-memory result fail.
